13	# Gkeyll guide
14	
15	## Directory structure
16	
17	Gkeyll has four PDE solvers: 
18	* Moments or fluid solver.
19	* Vlasov solver.
20	* Gyrokinetic solver.
21	* PKPM solver.
22	
23	Correspondingly, these solvers are organized into four separate folders, and they
24	share some common functionality in a fifth folder. Gkeyll is mostly organized in:
25	* core/: functionality common to all solvers.
26	* moments/: files for the moments solver.
27	* vlasov/: files for the Vlasov solver.
28	* gyrokinetic/: files for the gyrokinetic solver.
29	* pkpm/: files for the PKPM solver.
30	
31	Note that the four solvers are not independent. They have the following
32	dependencies:
33	* moments depends on core.
34	* vlasov depends on moments.
35	* gyrokinetic depends on vlasov.
36	* pkpm depends on gyrokinetic.
37	
38	Each of the solvers' folders have the sub-folders:
39	* ker/: C kernels generated with Maxima stored in the gkylcas repository. Do
40	  not modify, and if you think you should, please ask for permission.
41	* zero/: C and CUDA functions or modules (sometimes we call them updaters),
42	  some of which call kernels in ker/.
43	* data/: data needed for some simulations.
44	* unit/: unit tests of specific components in zero/.
45	* apps/: apps are called by input files or regression tests, and they organize
46	  solver workflow or simulations and call modules in zero/.
47	* creg/: C regression tests or short simulations to ensure solvers work (these
48	  are also examples of C input files).
49	* luareg/: Lua regression tests or short simulations to ensure solvers work
50	  (these are also examples of Lua input files).
51	
52	## Library dependencies
53	
54	The Gkeyll source code in gkeyll/ depends on other libraries installed in gkylsoft/.
55	Most of the time you shouldn't need to read files in gkylsoft/ unless prompted.
56	
57	## CPU - GPU organization
58	
59	Gkeyll runs on both CPUs and GPUs, the latter using CUDA.
60	- CPU-only implementations live in .c files.
61	- C files call host-side wrappers of CUDA kernels, both of which live in _cu.cu
62	  files.
63	
64	## Search hierarchy
65	
66	Rather than looking into the entire codebase without prior knowledge, look into
67	folders in the following order:
68	- Look into a folder (ending in /) the user referenced.
69	- If the user referenced a specific solver (e.g. gyrokinetic), look into its
70	  folder.
71	- Look into folders for solvers that the specified solver depends on, following
72	  the dependency chain up through core/.
73	
74	## Naming conventions.
75	
76	### Files.
77	
78	Gkeyll is written in C and CUDA, in addition to some Lua input files.
79	- Public header files have names starting with gkyl_ and ending in .h.
80	- Private header files have names starting with gkyl_ and ending in _priv.h.
81	- CUDA files have names ending in _cu.cu. 
82	- luareg/ folders have Lua input files whose names end with .lua. The Lua
83	  wrappers are in the apps/ folders and have names ending in _lw.c
84	
85	### Functions
86	
87	- Public functions (defined in public header files) should have a name that starts
88	  with gkyl_.
89	- Public functions in files in zero/ folders should have a name that starts
90	  with the name of the file that contains it.
91	- Private functions (defined in private header files) or static (and not defined
92	  in private headers) in files in zero/ folders should have a name that starts
93	  with an abbreviated version of the name of the file that contains it.
94	
95	### Variables
96	
97	- Do not use single letter names for variables whose scope spans more than ~15
98	  lines.
99	
100	## Module structure and pattern
101	
102	Most modules in zero/ or apps/ consist of 3 public functions:
103	1. A creation function, typically called gkyl_<module>_new or gkyl_<module>_init.
104	2. An execution function, typically called gkyl_<module>_advance or gkyl_<module>_apply.
105	3. A deletion function, typically called gkyl_<module>_release.
106	
107	There may also be some additional auxiliary private or public functions.
108	
109	## Building gkeyll
110	
111	Typicaly the library dependencies will already be installed, and to build Gkeyll
112	all you have to do is
113	
114	make -j3 install
115	
116	from the gkeyll/ folder.
117	
118	In order to compile unit regression tests you must give the makefile the target
119	executable, for example:
120	
121	make -j3 build/core/unit/ctest_gkyl_array
122	
123	Similarly, to build a regression test you would do, for example
124	
125	make -j3 build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
126	
127	## Running unit and regression tests
128	
129	Once the corresponding unit or regression test has been compiled, you can run
130	them from the gkeyll/ folder like:
131	
132	./build/core/unit/ctest_gkyl_array
133	./build/gyrokinetic/creg/rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1
134	
135	Regression tests can also run in parallel, preferably using the OpenMPI that
136	Gkeyll installed in gkylsoft/. For example, to run the rt_gk_sheath_2x2v_p1 on
137	4 cores you'd use (assuming you are in gkeyll/)

141	Here -M is needed to parallelize, and -c X -d Y -e Z are used to tell the

Based on the official OpenAI documentation and supporting sources, here's how Codex CLI skills and the SKILL.md format work:

## What a Skill Is
A skill is a directory with a SKILL.md file plus optional scripts and references, and the SKILL.md file must include name and description. Skills build on the open agent skills standard and are the authoring format for reusable workflows.

## Creating a Skill
You can create a skill manually by making a folder with a SKILL.md file containing frontmatter with name and description fields explaining exactly when the skill should and should not trigger, followed by the skill instructions body.

## Invocation Methods
Skills can be triggered two ways:
- **Explicit**: Include the skill directly in your prompt — in Codex CLI or the IDE extension, run /skills or type $ to mention a skill.
- **Implicit**: Codex can choose a skill when your task matches the skill description, so it's important to write concise descriptions with clear scope and boundaries since implicit matching depends on description.

## Directory Locations (Official Spec)
According to OpenAI's official docs, Codex reads skills from repository, user, admin, and system locations. For repositories, Codex scans .agents/skills in every directory from your current working directory up to the repository root.

The four scan locations are:
- **REPO**: $REPO_ROOT/.agents/skills — the topmost root folder when you launch Codex inside a Git repository, useful if organizations want skills relevant to everyone using the repository, serving as root skills available to any subfolder.
- **USER**: $HOME/.agents/skills — any skills checked into the user's personal folder, used to curate skills relevant to a user across any repository they work in.
- **ADMIN**: /etc/codex/skills — any skills checked into the machine or container in a shared, system location, used for SDK scripts, automation, and default admin skills available to each user on the machine.
- **SYSTEM**: Bundled with Codex by OpenAI.

Note: If two skills share the same name, Codex doesn't merge them; both can appear in skill selectors.

## Note on ~/.codex/skills/ vs .agents/skills/
There's some inconsistency across sources here worth flagging. The **official OpenAI docs** (developers.openai.com/codex/skills) specify `.agents/skills` as the standard path convention. However, several third-party sites (mdskills.ai, agensi.io, skills-hub.ai) describe `~/.codex/skills/` and `.codex/skills/` as the paths, and one blog post from personal testing found skills at `~/.codex/skills/.system/` where OpenAI ships some "global" skills in ~/.codex/skills/.system — a 'plan' skill and a 'skill-creator' skill, and you can drop your own global skills into ~/.codex/skills/. This suggests Codex CLI may support both path conventions, or the paths evolved over time — it's best to check `codex --version` documentation or run `/skills` in your session to confirm which paths your specific build scans.

## Progressive Disclosure (Context Efficiency)
Skills use progressive disclosure to manage context efficiently: Codex starts with each skill's name, description, and file path, and loads the full SKILL.md instructions only when it decides to use a skill, including an initial list of available skills in context so it can choose the right one for a task. To avoid crowding out the rest of the prompt, this list uses at most 2% of the model's context window (or 8,000 characters if unknown); if many skills are installed, Codex shortens descriptions first, and for large skill sets may omit some skills with a warning.

## Additional Notes
- Codex detects skill changes automatically, but if an update doesn't appear, you should restart Codex.
- Codex supports symlinked skill folders and follows the symlink target when scanning these locations.
- There's an allow_implicit_invocation setting (default: true) — when false, Codex won't implicitly invoke the skill based on user prompt, though explicit $skill invocation still works.
- Best practices include: keeping each skill focused on one job, preferring instructions over scripts unless you need deterministic behavior or external tooling, and writing imperative steps with explicit inputs and outputs.

That commit is already pushed to `origin/agent_tools`, which changes the calculus — cleanly removing the bad file content from the commit would mean amending and force-pushing, rewriting shared history.

Also, worth flagging the stash mechanics directly: `git stash` always resets the working tree to match HEAD for the paths it stashes. So if I just revert the file in the working tree and then stash it, that stash operation would put the *bad* (committed) version back on disk — the opposite of "reverted." To end up with the old version on disk **and** the bad changes safely in a stash, I'd need to actually rewrite the commit (amend it back to the old content) and then stash the bad diff on top separately.

options.description: Don't touch history. Revert the file's content in a new commit (so HEAD moves forward with old content restored), and separately save the bad diff to a stash. The old commit still has the bad version buried in history, but nothing is rewritten/force-pushed.
